overview: Czechoslovakia was created in 1918 from lands formerly within Austria-Hungary. It joined Czech lands, Slovakia and, in the interwar period, Carpathian Ruthenia. Its history included parliamentary democracy, wartime destruction, Communist rule and the peaceful separation into two republics at the end of 1992.

periods.title: The interwar republic
periods.summary: The republic lost border regions after the 1938 Munich agreement and was dismantled in 1939.

periods.title: Occupation, exile and resistance
periods.summary: Nazi Germany occupied the Czech lands; a separate Slovak state became an Axis client. Czechoslovak institutions also operated in exile.

periods.title: Restoration after war
periods.summary: Czechoslovakia was restored without Carpathian Ruthenia.

periods.title: Communist rule
periods.summary: The Communist takeover of 1948 changed political life; reform in 1968 was crushed by invasion.

periods.title: Democracy and separation
periods.summary: The Velvet Revolution ended Communist rule, followed by a negotiated division into the Czech and Slovak republics.

items.text: Bratislava’s new Comenius University opened its medical faculty in 1919. Professors arriving from Prague helped establish clinics for surgery, children’s medicine, dentistry and other specialties. Teaching in Czech and Slovak helped build a new generation of doctors in Slovakia.

Medical students needed physics as well as anatomy. In 1923/24, Bratislava began first-year teaching through a medical physics institute, initially housed in a grammar-school building. It moved into new university premises in 1926. A university could begin with borrowed rooms and grow laboratory by laboratory.

Young people arriving to work and train at Baťa’s shoe enterprise in Zlín could be only fourteen. Dormitories housed both young men and young women. The company’s organized world stretched beyond the factory gate into study, accommodation and daily routines.

Architect František Lydie Gahura used a repeating 6.15-meter concrete framework for the Zlín dormitories. Shared facilities occupied lower floors, with rooms above. The buildings belonged to a planned industrial town where even a bedroom followed an architectural system.

In 1961, chemist Otto Wichterle developed a way to cast soft contact lenses. The National Technical Museum preserves an early machine and material connected with the first production. Carefully controlled spinning could shape something small enough to sit on an eye.

Wichterle’s Christmas 1961 experiments used pieces of a Merkur construction set. Its metal strips, bolts and nuts had been familiar toys for decades. This was an unusually productive answer to “What did you build with your toys?”

The tramping movement grew around weekend escapes into the countryside, borrowing imagery from the American Wild West. Campers developed songs, nicknames and shared camps. You could leave the city for a small adventure without crossing the Atlantic.

Handwritten camp journals, illustrated chronicles, a carved totem and flags survive in museum collections. Some flags had been confiscated by Communist police. These objects preserve both the fun of belonging to a group and the times when authorities viewed independent gatherings with suspicion.

Prague’s House of Fashion opened in 1956. A checked cotton dress made by Módní závody Praha between 1956 and 1960 survives in the National Museum’s collection. Clothing history includes everyday fabrics and shop counters, as well as political speeches about how people should live.

The 1920 constitution gave adult citizens voting rights without distinction of sex. It also specified Sunday elections. Women could participate in national political life, although the law’s age requirements and other electoral conditions still mattered.

During the Prague Spring of 1968, Alexander Dubček’s leadership loosened controls and pursued reform. Soviet-led Warsaw Pact troops invaded in August. The effort to change Communism from within met military force, and the consequences reached classrooms, workplaces and public debate.

Czech, the 1920 constitution, section 1: “Lid je jediný zdroj veškeré státní moci v republice Československé.” Translation: “The people are the sole source of all state power in the Czechoslovak Republic.” Parliament preserves this historical wording, including the older form of the country’s name.

ending.text: Czechoslovakia ceased to exist at the end of 1992. The Czech Republic and Slovakia became separate states on 1 January 1993 through a peaceful political settlement. The map’s 1994 boundary is a snapshot transition, not the actual date of dissolution.
